Cost of Living | U.S. House of Representatives img {float: right;} </style> <p>As everyone in our Hawai‘i knows all too well, our state is consistently ranked as one of the most expensive in our country due to various factors. My focus has been on breaking down the overall high cost of living into its individual causes and then focusing on what our federal government can do to address each and all of these individual factors. These are a few of my actions on some of the major factors in the current 119th Congress.</p> <p><strong>Shipping&nbsp;Costs / Jones Act</strong></p> <p>The high cost of living in Hawai‘i is deeply tied to the high cost of shipping as we must import almost all our goods from the continent. Shipping costs in Hawai‘i are artificially high due to a 105-year-old federal shipping law known as the Jones Act, which mandates that all cargo between U.S. ports be transported on U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed ships. This has created monopolistic conditions by effectively shutting out international competitors and allowing just two companies to dominate the market. As a result, transportation costs are inflated and passed down to consumers, raising the price of essential goods like food and housing materials.</p> <p>This duopoly is especially problematic since Hawai‘i receives 90% of its goods by sea. The Jones Act adds around $1,800 a year to the average Hawai‘i family’s expenses and severely limits the state’s ability to develop affordable housing, support local industries like agriculture, or respond cost-effectively to emergencies.</p> <p>To address the major impact of the Jones Act on high costs, I have introduced three bills:</p> <ul style="list-style-type: disc;"> <li>The Noncontiguous Shipping Relief Act, which exempts noncontiguous regions (not part of the continent) from the Jones Act;</li> <li>the Noncontiguous Shipping Reasonable Rate Act, which caps domestic shipping rates to within 10% of international benchmarks; and</li> <li>The Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act, which allows noncontiguous regions to invite non-Jones Act vessels to restore competition an

Education | U.S. House of Representatives <span style="font-family: 'Segoe UI';">One of the core obligations of government is to assure that all of our our people can access a high-quality, affordable education. Our collective investment in education must start at life’s early stages and continue through an education that provides the skills necessary to earn a good living in a rapidly changing economy. The federal government has a major role in achieving this goal, and my own efforts are devoted to assuring that our federal government is provided the proper legislation and policies, along with sufficient funding, staff and other resources, to deliver across a variety of needs.<br /> </span> <h2><span style="font-family: 'Segoe UI'; font-size: 24px;"><strong>Focus on Appropriations</strong></span></h2> <p data-olk-copy-source="MessageBody"><span style="font-family: 'Segoe UI';"><span style="font-size: 16px;">Education is one of my major focuses in our U.S. Committee on Appropriations, on which I have served since my return to Congress in 2019. Appropriations is responsible for funding and overseeing all discretionary federal education efforts. Over the years I have worked to secure funding for a wide range of education programs that help our state.
